Messages.Author: Steve Wampler
Messages.Body:
In hopes of prompting a discussion that will illuminate some areas of
other discussions....

In the recent discussions about weenie decks, many people have
complained that they are "boring" and/or repetitive because each weenie
vampire bleeds every turn. IMNSHO, this is a sign that these people are
unused to playing *really* competitive decks.

Quite simply, the very structure of Jyhad favors decks which, when they
play a given card, generally draw the same or a very similar card as a
replacement.

A deck with a wide variety of cards so that you can *potentially* deal
with any given situation will lose 90% of the time to a deck which
consistently creates one situation and takes advantage of it.
Examples:
1) A rush deck creates many, many, combats and has cards in the deck
which allow it to consistantly destroy its opponents, which are
carefully picked so that their death swings the balance of power towards
the rush deck. A deck with light combat will inevitably find that it
doesn't have the combat cards it needs when it needs them and that they
jam its hand at other times.
2) A vote deck calls many, many votes and has other cards which grant
votes, so that any given vote will pass or fail based upon whether on
not it would be to the vote decks advantage. Decks with light vote
power tend to be unable to pass their votes and in the situations when
they do have vote control, they rarely draw enough useful votes to be
threatening.
3) Cryptic Mission decks have enough CMs to drain opposing vamps
completely dry, then either slay them with SoL or just render them
useless. A tremere deck with just a couple of CMs will find them a
waste most of the time.

As far as defenses go, it is far more effective to either
1) Be able to stop any sort of action, regardless of type
-or-
2) Not care what your opponent has in mind

Intercept decks block anything and everything. Rush decks and CM decks
prevent vampires from doing anything. MT/5th decks gain so much pool
that it doesn't matter what other people are doing to them.

Other points will likely be brought up if this thread continues.

The best decks, regardless of concept, do the same things over and
over. This is simply a natural result of people building decks that are
designed to win given the rules set. People who want huge variety might
prefer playing VtM.

--
Steve Wampler

Having avoided the newsgroup due to the sheer lack of anything useful to
say, I'm afraid I can't add very much to the discussion, except for the
*mother* of all repetitive decks... the "Recycling Aurora" deck. Thus,
to the point of this post: to introduce to the "Recycling Aurora" deck
all those who have not yet made it's aquaintance. Basically, your crypt
consists of as many Aurora Van Brande as you can lay your grubby little
hands on. In JOL, that means approximately a 100-card crypt. Aurora
equips the Soul Gem, and a Camarilla Vitae Slave, then bleeds with
either GtU or FoW, adding in Threats or Conditioning (as blood permits),
and a Daring the Dawn. She then turns to extremely crispy toast. Enter
Aurora Van Brande #2 (or 3 or 4 or...), untapped, full of blood, and
still holding the Soul Gem, get another Vitae Slave, lather, rinse,
repeat. If the deck gets a lucky draw, it's sweep the table in a turn
time. Granted, it's rather unlikely, but I think it at least draws a
nice counter-argument to the "repetitive decks are boring" thing,
dontcha think? 8)

-Chris Berger

Aurora with a Camarilla Vitae Slave is a 7 capacity vampire (Aurora's 6
plus CVS's "increase her capacity by 1"). The next Aurora in the crypt
is a 6.

A 7 capacity vampire is older than a 6 capacity vampire [1.5.2]
This applies for all purposes, including Soul Gem.

Messages.Author: pie...@my-deja.com
Messages.Body:
> Or if you ever end up in torpor. A rush deck will clean you up,
> and a deck with even light intercept will screw you. You can't
> get the Vitae Slave and the Soul Gem on the same action --
> and you need them both.

Torpor is a problem because then people just leave you there.
You can always contest with yourself but this slows you down too much.

The theory, I believe, is as follows:
Turn 1
-up to 4 transfers to Aurora1
Turn 2
-up to 4 transfers to Aurora1 to bring her out
-Any remaining transfers to Aurora2 in case you are screwed.
Turn 3
Equip Aurora1 with Soul Gem of Etrius.
Freak Drive or not as you like to manage the hand.
-transfer to Aurora2 until she has two blood as needed.
Turn 4
Equip with a Camarilla Vitae Slave (Costs two blood)
Add a Shroud of night as needed - +2 Stealth - Costs one blood
Freak Drive (Costs one blood)
Mind Rape (inferior) Bleed with +2 bleed (Costs two blood)
With Conditioning + bleed (costs one blood)
With Shroud of night as needed to continue burning blood and managing
the hand.
Add Daring the Dawn taking two agg and burning at the end of the action.

Aurora5 comes out - repeat from beginning of turn 4 until the hand jams
with something you don't want.

-
Blood management
CVS 2
Freak Drive 1
Mind Rape 2
Conditioning 1
Shroud of Night 1

Aurora has a 6 cap and all of those cards cost a total of 7 so you
cannot play all of those cards. The Shroud is the issue. You might
need the stealth, you might not.

Therefore, I would reccomend:
QTY Card
14 Camarilla Vitae Slave
14 Freak Drive
14 Mind Rape
14 Conditioning
14 Daring the Dawn
7 Shadow Play
7 Soul Gem
6 Deal with the Devil
---------------------------
90 TOTAL

and about 20 Aurora's just to be sure you have enough.
More than 18 is technically unnecessary since you will only burn 14
yourself and have four in the initial crypt, ending you with one full
Aurora at the end of your library.

Just my 2 pool.
Thanks
Stu
